courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Memory cost, ablations, failure modes and gsplat in practice
question: You need to stream a 3DGS scene to phones and your budget is tight. Which change cuts the most storage per Gaussian while keeping geometry intact?
options: Drop the quaternion and use isotropic Gaussians
Store opacity in 8 bits instead of 32
Reduce SH degree from 3 to 0 or 1, giving up some view-dependent color
Remove the position and infer it from the sort order
explain: 48 of the 59 floats are SH color. Dropping to degree 0 keeps 14 floats (168 MB instead of 708 MB at 3 million Gaussians). Isotropic Gaussians save only 6 floats and hurt geometry; the paper's ablation shows anisotropy matters.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks
question: A thread can be suspended for minutes inside a data structure operation (for example, it is stopped by a debugger or swapped out). You must keep memory bounded. Which scheme fits?
options: Hazard pointers, because a stalled thread can block reclamation of only the nodes it has announced
Epoch-based reclamation, because it has the lowest per-access cost
A 16-bit tagged pointer with nodes freed immediately
explain: Michael proves at most N times R retired nodes stay unreclaimed regardless of stalls. Epochs stop advancing while the stalled thread sits in a critical region, so all garbage is retained. Freeing tagged nodes immediately lets the stale read of next touch freed memory, and 16-bit tags can wrap.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Reporting an ablation people can trust
question: You ran all 16 configurations of a 4-stage pipeline and tested every pair at alpha = 0.05 with independent paired t-tests. Three pairs come out significant. What is the main concern?
options: Paired t-tests cannot be used for nDCG
With 120 tests, several false positives are expected by chance; plan the comparisons or use a procedure such as Tukey's HSD
Sixteen configurations are too few for a full factorial design
The result is fine as long as the three pairs share a stage
explain: At 0.05 per test, 120 tests yield about 6 false positives on average even if nothing differs. Restrict to planned comparisons (leave-one-out rows, suspected interactions) or control the familywise error.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Case: First American Financial and 885 million documents (2019)
question: A colleague proposes fixing a First American style document viewer by switching from sequential numbers to random 128-bit ids, with no other change. What is still wrong?
options: Nothing; random ids are unguessable so the problem is solved
Random ids are slower to look up
Any link that is forwarded, logged or leaked still opens the document for anyone, because nothing checks who is asking
128 bits is too short
explain: Random ids stop guessing, but a link still acts as the only credential. Emails get forwarded, URLs land in logs and browser history. An authorization check tied to a logged-in recipient is what limits who can open it (next lesson).

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Mass assignment and property-level authorization
question: A ModelForm uses `fields = "__all__"`. Today the model only has display_name and bio. Next month a teammate adds `is_staff_reviewed`. What happens?
options: Nothing; Django ignores new fields in existing forms
Django raises an error until the form is updated
The new field becomes user-editable through the form without anyone touching the form code
The new field is shown but cannot be saved
explain: `__all__` means all fields at the time the form class is built, so new model fields join automatically. That is exactly the risk Django's docs warn about when they recommend listing fields explicitly.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Testing authorization with role matrices, and detecting enumeration
question: Feature tests pass for an invoices endpoint: the owner can read their invoice. What additional test catches an IDOR?
options: Request the same invoice as the owner twice
Log in as a different user (and a user from another tenant) and request the owner's invoice id, expecting 404 or 403
Request an invoice id that does not exist
Load-test the endpoint
explain: IDOR is about the wrong user getting an object. Only a test that uses a second identity against the first user's object exercises the object-level check.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: NTLM relay: forwarding someone else's login, and how signing stops it
question: Why does requiring SMB signing defeat an SMB relay even though the relayed AUTHENTICATE message was valid?
options: Signing encrypts the challenge so it cannot be copied
Signing blocks LLMNR
Messages after sign-in must be signed with a session key derived from the victim's secret, which the relayer never learns
Signing forces Kerberos for every connection
explain: The relayer can forward the authentication but cannot compute the session key. Without it, it cannot produce valid signatures on the requests it wants to send.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Delegation: letting a server act as you, and how it goes wrong
question: A file server has unconstrained delegation. A Domain Admin opens a share on it. Why is that dangerous if the server is later compromised?
options: The admin's password is written to the share
The server becomes a domain controller
A forwarded copy of the admin's TGT sits on the server and can be used to request tickets to any service as the admin
Unconstrained delegation disables Kerberos encryption
explain: With unconstrained delegation the client forwards its TGT to the service. Whoever controls the server can reuse it until it expires.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AD CS: when a certificate template hands out admin
question: Which single template setting is the crux of ESC1?
options: The certificate is valid for one year
The template uses SHA-256
The requester may supply the subject alternative name
The CA is online
explain: If the requester writes the SAN, a low-privileged user can request a certificate naming any account. The other conditions (enrollment rights, no approval, an authentication EKU) make it usable.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: The exploit lifecycle: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload
question: In Brandon Azad's terminology, return-oriented programming is best described as which of these?
options: An exploit technique that turns one primitive into a stronger one
An exploit primitive granted directly by a bug
An exploit strategy specific to one vulnerability
An exploit flow covering the whole attack
explain: Azad uses ROP as the example of an exploit technique: a reusable method that turns control of the program counter into nearly arbitrary code execution. It does not depend on which bug provided the control.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: When control flow stays legal: data-only attacks
question: A codebase enables fine-grained CFI, shadow stacks and PAC. An overflow can change a neighbouring permissions field but no code pointers. What protects it?
options: Nothing in that list; the program follows legal edges. A bounds fix, memory tagging or moving the field out of reach is needed
CFI, because permissions checks are indirect calls
The shadow stack, because the overflow is on the stack
PAC, because it signs all data
explain: Chen et al. showed such non-control-data attacks give compromises equivalent to control hijacks. All three listed defences validate control transfers, and none of them is violated here.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: JIT and browser engine bugs, and the V8 sandbox
question: Why would rewriting V8's runtime in a memory-safe language not stop JIT type-confusion bugs, according to the V8 team?
options: Because the corruption is done by machine code the JIT generates from a wrong assumption, and the source language of the compiler does not make its output correct
Because Rust cannot run JavaScript
Because JIT bugs are hardware bugs
Because memory-safe languages forbid optimization
explain: The bug is in the compiler's reasoning. The compiler can be perfectly memory safe and still emit code that skips a needed check. That is why V8 chose to contain corruption (the sandbox) instead of trying to prevent it everywhere.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Zero-click chains: FORCEDENTRY and Operation Triangulation
question: Why did pointer authentication and memory tagging have no effect on FORCEDENTRY's sandbox escape, according to Project Zero?
options: Because the escape used only logic bugs in object serialization features, with no memory corruption for those checks to catch
Because the device did not support them
Because the escape ran in the kernel
Because tagging was in asynchronous mode
explain: PAC and MTE detect forged pointers and mismatched memory accesses. A chain made of legitimate features used in unintended ways never triggers either, which is why attack-surface reduction matters as much as memory safety.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: SWE-bench: how one patch gets graded
question: A patch applies cleanly, makes both FAIL_TO_PASS tests pass, and causes one FAIL_TO_FAIL test to start passing, but one PASS_TO_PASS test now fails. Verdict?
options: Resolved, since the issue tests pass
Resolved with partial credit
Not resolved, because a PASS_TO_PASS test fails
Not graded, because FAIL_TO_FAIL changed
explain: The verdict is binary and needs all FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS tests to pass. FAIL_TO_FAIL tests are ignored either way, and there is no partial credit.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: From one model call to an agent loop
question: A support bot always classifies a ticket, then calls exactly one of three fixed handlers. In the terms of Building effective agents, what is it?
options: An agent, because it uses an LLM to make a decision
A workflow (routing), because the code path is predefined
An augmented LLM, because it has no tools
An orchestrator-workers agent, because it delegates
explain: The control flow is fixed in code: classify, then dispatch. That is the routing workflow. It becomes an agent only when the model decides at runtime which steps to take and how many.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Permissions, traces and evaluation
question: Your agent passes 3 of 4 trials per task. Product needs it to succeed on every one of 5 consecutive uses. Roughly what reliability should you expect?
options: About 75 percent, the per-trial rate
About 24 percent, since 0.75 to the 5th power is 0.237
About 99.9 percent, since pass@5 is high
Exactly 60 percent
explain: Needing all 5 to succeed is pass^5 = 0.75^5, about 0.237. pass@5 answers a different question (at least one success) and is far too optimistic for a workflow that must succeed every time.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The read path: scoring memories by recency, importance and relevance
question: Generative Agents measures recency from a memory's last *access*, not its creation. After this query retrieves M6, M5, M3, M1 and M7, what happens on the next query an hour later?
options: Nothing changes; recency only depends on creation time
The retrieved memories get recency 0.995 raw, so they gain an edge: frequently retrieved memories tend to stay retrievable
The retrieved memories are demoted so the agent sees different ones next time
Importance is re-rated for the retrieved memories
explain: Retrieval updates the last-access timestamp, so one hour later those five have raw recency 0.995 while the rest keep decaying. This is a rich-get-richer effect: it keeps active topics in view, but it can also lock in an early mistake. Importance is rated once, at creation.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Layer the checks: deterministic first, judges last
question: An agent fills a booking form and must output JSON with a date, a flight number in a fixed format, and a price within the user's budget. Which verification plan fits best?
options: Ask a strong LLM judge whether the booking looks right, since it can check all three fields at once
Validate the JSON schema and regex, check the price and date with code, then use a judge only for whether the flight matches the user's stated preferences
Re-ask the same agent to double-check its JSON before submitting
Skip checks for the format and only verify the price, since format errors are rare
explain: Format, ranges and arithmetic are deterministic: code checks them exactly and almost for free. A judge is reserved for the fuzzy part (preferences) that code cannot express.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Multi-turn rollouts: one sequence, two authors, one loss mask
question: In the toy rollout, the loss is normalized by the number of masked-in tokens. How many tokens is that, and what fraction of the sequence?
options: 20 tokens, 100 percent, since every token is part of the episode
16 tokens, 80 percent: everything after the prompt
6 tokens, 30 percent: only the tool outputs
10 tokens, 50 percent: only the policy's own tokens
explain: 4 prompt tokens and 6 tool tokens are masked out, leaving the 10 tokens the model sampled across its three turns. Including tool tokens would turn the update into imitation of environment text.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: The map: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025
question: An internal chatbot answers "what is my manager's salary?" by retrieving an HR spreadsheet that the asking employee is not allowed to open. Which entry fits best?
options: LLM10 Unbounded Consumption
LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
LLM03 Supply Chain
LLM09 Misinformation
explain: The retrieval layer ignored the user's permissions. OWASP lists unauthorised access and cross-user leakage from vector stores under LLM08, with permission-aware retrieval as the fix. It also ends as LLM02 disclosure, but the weakness is in retrieval.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Getting data out: images, links, tool calls
question: In the Slack AI case, which missing control would have most directly prevented the leak?
options: Stronger passwords for Slack accounts
Encrypting the private channel at rest
Not rendering model-generated links to unapproved domains, and keeping untrusted public-channel text out of answers that use private data
Rate limiting Slack AI queries
explain: The data left through a rendered link to an attacker domain, and the instruction came from untrusted public content mixed with private data. Removing the exit or separating the contexts breaks the chain; encryption at rest does nothing once the assistant itself reads the key.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: System prompt leakage and sensitive information disclosure
question: A banking chatbot's system prompt says: "Users with role=gold may transfer up to 50,000 without extra checks." What is the core problem?
options: The limit is too high
The prompt might leak
An authorisation rule is enforced by the model instead of by deterministic code in the transfer service
The prompt should be in another language
explain: OWASP's point for LLM07: disclosure is a symptom. The real flaw is delegating authorisation to the model, which can be talked out of it. The transfer service must check the role and limit itself.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Misinformation and unbounded consumption
question: A chatbot's answer contradicts the company's published policy and a customer relies on it. Based on Moffatt v. Air Canada, who is responsible?
options: Nobody, because AI output is unpredictable
The chatbot vendor only
The customer, for not reading the policy page
The company that runs the chatbot on its website
explain: The tribunal held that the chatbot is part of Air Canada's website and the company is responsible for all information on it, whatever the source.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: A crystal as data: lattice, fractional coordinates, periodicity
question: A teammate builds neighbor lists for a crystal GNN by computing Euclidean distances between Cartesian positions inside one unit cell only. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, since the unit cell already contains every atom of the crystal
Atoms near opposite faces of the cell look far apart, so real short bonds across the boundary are missing from the graph
Distances come out in fractional units instead of angstrom
The hexagonal lattice cannot be represented, only cubic ones
explain: The cell contains one copy of each atom, but its neighbors include periodic images in adjacent cells. Without minimum image (or explicit image enumeration), P and Q at 0.05 and 0.95 look 3.6 angstrom apart instead of 0.4 angstrom. CDVAE notes its networks explicitly encode interactions across periodic boundaries for this reason.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Why AI text needs a planted signal
question: Which output would be hardest to watermark, whatever scheme you use?
options: A short story written from an open-ended prompt
A list of brainstormed product names
The first 50 digits of pi, written out exactly
A casual email reply
explain: A watermark can only act where the model has real choices. The digits of pi are fully determined, so the watermarked model must produce the same tokens a human would, leaving no room for a signal. Open-ended prose has high entropy and is easy to mark.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Capturing calls: glibc mtrace and LD_PRELOAD interposers
question: On a glibc 2.39 system, a program calls mtrace() first thing, MALLOC_TRACE=/tmp/t is set and /tmp is writable, but no trace appears. What is the most likely cause?
options: mtrace() only works when the program is compiled with -g
libc_malloc_debug.so was not preloaded, so mtrace() is a no-op
The program must also call muntrace() to flush the file
MALLOC_TRACE must point to a directory, not a file
explain: Since glibc 2.34, mtrace and the two heap-checking features mcheck and MALLOC_CHECK_ live in libc_malloc_debug.so and are disabled in the main library. -g only improves the file:line output, and the docs advise never calling muntrace().

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
question: Why does the modified z-score multiply by 0.6745?
options: It converts the MAD into a 95 percent confidence interval
It corrects for small sample sizes the way n-1 does in the standard deviation
For normal data the MAD is about 0.6745 standard deviations, so the scaling makes M read like a z-score
It is the fraction of points the median ignores
explain: For normal data the median of |x - mu| (the MAD) is about 0.6745 sigma, because 0.6745 is the 75th percentile of the standard normal. Dividing by MAD and multiplying by 0.6745 is the same as dividing by an outlier-resistant estimate of sigma (MAD x 1.4826).

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: API keys, bearer tokens and session cookies
question: Security wants to cut off a stolen token within seconds. Which design makes that easiest?
options: Long-lived self-contained JWTs with no lookup
API keys that never expire
Putting the token in a cookie
Opaque tokens checked against the issuer (introspection), or very short-lived JWTs backed by a revocable refresh token
explain: A token that is looked up can be deleted. A self-contained token stays valid until its exp unless every API checks a revocation list, which removes most of its advantage. Short lifetimes shrink that window.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: The authorization code flow with PKCE, step by step
question: An authorization server receives a token request with a valid code and a code_verifier, but no challenge was sent when that code was requested. What should it do?
options: Accept: the verifier proves possession
Accept, but log a warning
Reject: RFC 9700 says to accept a code_verifier only if a code_challenge was present, to stop PKCE downgrade
Ask the user to log in again
explain: If servers accepted a verifier with no challenge on record, an attacker could start the flow without PKCE and still look PKCE-compliant later. The verifier means nothing without the earlier commitment.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: JWT anatomy: header, payload, signature and base64url
question: A JWT header decodes to `{"alg":"RS256","kid":"k7"}`. What does the signature let a receiver confirm?
options: That the holder is the user named in sub
That header and payload were not changed since the holder of the private key for k7 signed them, once the receiver checks k7 is one of its trusted issuer's keys
That the payload is secret
That the token has not expired
explain: A signature proves origin and integrity of the signed bytes, nothing more. Possession is not identity (bearer token), expiry is a separate claim check, and secrecy needs encryption.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Storing tokens in browsers, short lifetimes and revocation
question: Your single-page app (SPA) keeps its access and refresh tokens in localStorage. An XSS bug is found. What should you assume?
options: Nothing leaked, since localStorage is per origin
Only the access token leaked
Both tokens may have been read and sent elsewhere; revoke the refresh tokens, fix the XSS, and consider moving to a BFF
Only users on old browsers are affected
explain: Same-origin script can read localStorage in full. The refresh token is the valuable one, since it mints new access tokens; revoke them (all, if you cannot scope the exposure) and fix the injection.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Three maps of a secure SDLC: Microsoft SDL, OWASP SAMM, NIST SSDF
question: In SSDF terms, running a vulnerability disclosure programme falls under which group?
options: PO, Prepare the Organization
PS, Protect the Software
PW, Produce Well-Secured Software
RV, Respond to Vulnerabilities
explain: Task RV.1.3 is having a policy for vulnerability disclosure and remediation. RV covers everything after release: finding residual vulnerabilities, fixing them and preventing repeats.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: How static analysis finds bugs: taint from source to sink
question: A developer writes `name = request.args.get('name').strip()` and then `cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM t WHERE name = '" + name + "'")`. What will a taint tool report, and is it right?
options: Nothing: strip() is a sanitiser
A false positive, because names are harmless
A finding: strip() only removes whitespace, so taint propagates to the sink, and the report is a true positive
Nothing: cursor.execute is not a sink
explain: strip() returns a modified copy of tainted text, so the result is still tainted. Only operations whose output cannot carry the attack, such as int() for SQL or encoding for HTML, are sanitisers.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Secrets scanning and pre-commit hooks
question: A developer committed an API key, noticed, and pushed a second commit deleting it within a minute. What is the correct response?
options: None: the key is gone from the latest version
Make the repository private
Revoke the key at the provider, issue a new one, and check the key's usage logs
Squash the two commits
explain: The key is still in the first commit, and pushed history may already be cloned. Only revoking it removes its power. Then look for use between push and revocation.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Prioritising with CVSS, EPSS and KEV, computed on real CVEs
question: A finding has CVSS 9.8, EPSS 0.007, is not in KEV, and runs on an internal tool reachable only from the corporate network. Another has CVSS 7.5, is in KEV, and runs on an internet-facing proxy. Which goes first, and why?
options: The 9.8, because severity is what matters
The 7.5 in KEV on the internet-facing proxy, because it is being exploited and is exposed
Both equally
Neither until a pentest confirms them
explain: This is CVE-2023-44487 against CVE-2024-2057 in the example. Exploitation evidence plus exposure beats a theoretical maximum score. The 9.8 still gets fixed, on the normal schedule.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Why a crash needs both undo and redo
question: A system uses no-steal and no-force. After a crash, which work can recovery skip entirely?
options: Redo of committed transactions, because their pages were written at commit
Undo of uncommitted transactions, because their changes never reached the data pages
Both, because the log already contains everything
Neither, because the log may be incomplete
explain: No-steal guarantees no uncommitted change was ever written to a data page, so there is nothing to undo. No-force means committed changes may still be missing on disk, so redo is still required.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
question: One page, all records for it. Before the crash: updates 1 and 2, the page is written to disk, updates 3 and 4, a partial rollback writes CLRs 4' and 3', then updates 5 and 6. The transaction is a loser. What does ARIES do at restart?
options: Redo nothing, since the transaction is a loser; undo 6, 5, 2, 1
Redo 1 through 6; undo 6, 5, 4', 3'
explain: This is Fig. 13 of the ARIES paper. Redo repeats everything after the page write, CLRs included. Undo follows PrevLSN from 6 to 5, then reaches CLR 3', whose UndoNextLSN points at 2, so 4 and 3 are not undone again. Then 2 and 1.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Input-type bugs in real pipelines
question: You want to cluster 50,000 support tickets by topic with an API that offers search_query, search_document, classification and clustering types. Which setup matches the docs?
options: search_query for half the tickets and search_document for the other half
The clustering type for every ticket
search_document for all tickets, since they are stored documents
No input type, because clustering does not use cosine
explain: Clustering compares tickets with each other, a symmetric task, so every text gets the same role. Cohere documents a clustering type for exactly this, and Nomic uses a clustering prefix on both sides. Splitting the tickets across query and document types would make the halves systematically different.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Retries that do not stampede: backoff, jitter and Retry-After
question: A 429 arrives with `Retry-After: 30`. Your backoff ceiling for this attempt would be 0.8 s. What should the client do?
options: Sleep a random time in [0, 0.8] s, since full jitter is best
Sleep 0.8 s, then 30 s if the next attempt fails
Wait at least 30 s, with a little added randomness, before retrying
Ignore the header; it is only used with 503
explain: Retry-After is the server telling you when capacity will be back. RFC 6585 allows it on 429, Anthropic says to wait that many seconds, and OpenAI treats it as a minimum and suggests adding a small random delay. Retrying after 0.8 s just produces another 429 and spends request budget.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Why waiting on threads is expensive and coroutines are cheap
question: What makes Rust's `async fn` a *stackless* coroutine?
options: It cannot call other functions
It runs on the caller's stack forever and never suspends
It suspends by returning to its caller, and the data needed to resume lives in a separate object
It is only allowed inside a runtime with one thread
explain: Stackless means no private stack: suspending is a return, and the locals that must survive the suspension are stored in a separate state object (the future). Stackful coroutines instead keep a whole stack per coroutine.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
question: Two threads each run a plain (non-atomic) `counter++` once on a shared counter that starts at 0. Which statement is right?
options: The result is always 2, because each increment is one machine instruction on x86
The result is 1 or 2, and in C or C++ the program has undefined behavior
The result is always 1, because both threads read 0
It is safe as long as the counter is declared volatile
explain: Depending on the schedule, both reads can happen before either write (result 1) or not (result 2). Being one x86 instruction does not help: the core still loads and stores separately. And since the accesses conflict without synchronization, the C++ standard calls this a data race, which is undefined behavior. volatile does not make it atomic.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
question: Using the same padding rule, how many YAMNet patches (score rows) does a 10.0 s clip produce?
options: 10, one per second
21, because the last partial hop adds an extra patch
explain: The 10 s clip is padded to 161,520 samples, giving 1008 STFT frames and $1 + \lfloor (1008 - 96)/48 \rfloor = 20$ patches. Twenty patches at a 0.48 s hop span 0 to 10.08 s.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: AST and SpecAugment: patches, attention and masked bands
question: A teammate implements frequency masking by writing -80 (very quiet in their dB scale) into masked bins of unnormalized log-mel features. What is the problem?
options: Nothing, silence is the most natural mask value
Masks must be applied to the waveform, not the spectrogram
Frequency masks must always cover exactly F bins
The masked block becomes an extreme, easy-to-spot value instead of the mean; SpecAugment normalizes to zero mean so 0 equals the mean
explain: In the paper, features are normalized to zero mean and masked values are set to 0, which is the mean. Filling with an extreme value creates an unnatural pattern the model can learn to detect, and it shifts the input statistics compared with test time.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Precomputed tables, rainbow tables, and why salts defeat them
question: Which attack does a per-user salt NOT slow down?
options: Looking a hash up in a precomputed rainbow table
Running a wordlist against a single targeted user's salted hash
Cracking a million users' hashes with one shared pass of a wordlist
Spotting which users share the same password
explain: For one user, the attacker just includes that user's salt in each guess; the cost is the same as an unsalted hash of that user. Only a slow hash raises the cost per guess.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: After login: session tokens, fixation, expiry and logout
question: An attacker steals a session cookie and runs a script that makes a request every minute. Which control limits how long the stolen session works?
options: Idle timeout
The SameSite attribute
Clearing the cookie when the victim closes the browser
Absolute timeout
explain: Constant activity keeps the idle timer reset forever. Only an absolute timeout ends the session a fixed time after login regardless of activity. Clearing the victim's copy does nothing to the attacker's copy.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Real-time phishing proxies and help-desk social engineering
question: A caller to your help desk knows an employee's ID, manager's name and last four digits of their social security number, and asks to move MFA to a new phone. Which response best follows the guidance for this threat?
options: Approve it: the caller knew three private facts
Verify identity on camera or by calling back a registered number, with the strictest checks for privileged accounts
Approve it, then email the employee afterwards
Reset the password but leave MFA unchanged
explain: Mandiant's guidance warns that this group often already has data like date of birth and the last four digits of a social security number, so such facts prove nothing. It asks for positive identity verification, such as on-camera checks or a call-back to a registered number, before any MFA or password change.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Orchestrator, parallel subagents and context isolation
question: Which task benefits least from an orchestrator with parallel subagents?
options: Collecting board members of every company in a large index
Comparing five databases on four criteria
A refactor where every change depends on the previous edit to the same files
Surveying literature on three independent sub-topics
explain: Parallel subagents pay off when work splits into independent pieces with separate contexts. A chain of dependent edits to shared files needs shared context and tight coordination, the case Anthropic says is not a good fit today.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Evaluating research agents without fooling yourself
question: Your research agent's LLM judge score rises from 0.71 to 0.83 after a prompt change. Which check most directly guards against fooling yourself?
options: Read a sample of transcripts and verify a few citations by hand to confirm the gain is real
Increase the eval set from 20 to 2,000 queries before looking at anything
Switch to a larger judge model and re-run
Accept the change: LLM judges are aligned with humans
explain: A judge score can rise because the agent learned to please the judge (confident tone, more citations) without being more correct. Spot-checking transcripts and citations by hand tests whether the improvement is real. A bigger eval set is useful later but does not detect a judge blind spot.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Building blocks: routing, prompt optimization, RAG, agents, guardrails
question: A user reports a wrong answer from your RAG app built on RetrieveAndGenerate. What in the response helps you debug it first?
options: The citations, which map parts of the answer to retrieved source chunks
usage.outputTokens
The guardrail trace only
stopReason
explain: Citations tie spans of the generated answer to retrieved references, so you can see whether retrieval found the wrong chunks or the model misread the right ones.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Training from scratch: latent weights and the STE
question: Halfway through training, the BitNet b1.58 recipe sets weight decay to 0. Why does that help a ternary model in particular?
options: Weight decay is incompatible with the STE gradient
Weight decay shrinks latent weights toward the rounding threshold, so ternary values keep flipping; removing it lets them settle
Weight decay would push ternary values toward 2
It saves optimizer memory
explain: The latent weight's magnitude acts as confidence in its ternary value. Decay keeps pulling magnitudes down toward the |w| < gamma/2 band, causing frequent flips. With decay off and a lower learning rate, the ternary weights can converge.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Global history, gshare, TAGE and perceptron predictors
question: Why does gshare XOR the address and history instead of just using the history bits as the index?
options: Using only history would make every branch with the same recent history share one counter
XOR is faster to compute than concatenation
XOR removes the need for 2-bit counters
It lets the predictor guess branch targets
explain: With history alone, all branches that just saw the same outcomes collide on one counter. Mixing in address bits spreads different branches across the table while still letting every history bit affect the index.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: B+trees update in place, and random writes pay for it
question: A B+tree index has 4 levels and the top 3 are cached. A workload switches from point lookups to random 100-byte updates on a table 50x larger than RAM. What dominates the new cost?
options: Extra disk reads to traverse the inner nodes
CPU time spent on binary search within pages
Rewriting a full page at a random location for each small update
Rebalancing the tree after every update
explain: Inner nodes are cached, so traversal stays cheap. Each update still needs its leaf read (one random read) and eventually a full-page random write. Updates in place do not change the tree shape, so no rebalancing happens.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: The buffer pool: frames, a page table, pins and dirty pages
question: A pool has 4 frames. All 4 pages are pinned by running queries, and a fifth query misses on a new page. What should a correct buffer manager do?
options: Evict the least recently used page anyway, since it is the best guess
Report that no frame is available, or make the request wait, because pinned pages cannot be evicted
Evict any dirty page after writing it back, because writing makes eviction safe
Pick a random page, since all are equally valid victims
explain: Pinned means some thread is reading or writing that frame right now; evicting it would pull memory out from under that thread. PostgreSQL's clock-sweep raises the error "no unpinned buffers available" if it scans every buffer and all are pinned. Writing a dirty page back does not make it unpinned.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: 2Q, InnoDB midpoint insertion and PostgreSQL ring buffers
question: A PostgreSQL job runs `UPDATE big_table SET flag = true` over every row of a table much larger than shared_buffers. Why can it still pollute the buffer pool despite ring buffers?
options: Ring buffers are only used for indexes
UPDATE always bypasses shared_buffers
Each ring buffer it uses gets dirtied, and a dirtied scan buffer is dropped from the ring and replaced through normal clock-sweep, so the ring degrades to the normal strategy
The ring is larger than shared_buffers
explain: The README says this directly: a scan that modifies every page dirties every ring buffer, and rather than flushing WAL to reuse it, the buffer is discarded from the ring and a replacement comes from the normal clock-sweep.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Inside BLT: local encoder, latent Transformer, local decoder
question: The n-gram 'cat' and some unrelated 3-gram hash to the same slot of $E_3^{hash}$. What happens?
options: Training fails with a key error
They share one embedding vector; the byte embedding and other n-gram sizes still distinguish them
The model falls back to a BPE tokenizer for that word
BLT rehashes until the slot is free
explain: Hash embeddings accept collisions: both n-grams add the same learned vector. Each position also gets its own byte embedding and five other n-gram lookups, and later layers see the context, so collisions only cost a little. Bigger tables reduce them.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: unsafe: five extra powers, same borrow checker
question: Which line needs an `unsafe` block?
options: `let p = 0x1000usize as *const u8;`
`let n = v.len();` on a `Vec<u8>`
`v.set_len(4);` on a `Vec<u8>`
`let r = &raw const x;`
explain: Creating raw pointers (by cast or with `&raw`) is safe: nothing happens until you dereference. `set_len` is an `unsafe fn` because it trusts you that the new length is within capacity and the elements are initialized, so calling it needs an unsafe block.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
question: An array holds 1,000,000 structs of 64 bytes each, line-aligned. A loop sums one 8-byte field from every struct. Roughly how many cache lines does one pass bring in, and what if that field lived in its own `double[1000000]` array instead?
options: 125,000 lines either way, since only 8 MB of values are read
1,000,000 lines for the structs; 125,000 for the separate array
1,000,000 lines either way, one per element
64,000,000 lines for the structs; 1,000,000 for the array
explain: Each struct is one full line, so reading any field of it fetches that line: 1,000,000 lines (64 MB). Packed into their own array, 8 values share each line: 1,000,000 / 8 = 125,000 lines (8 MB). Same values, 8x less traffic. This is the idea behind struct-of-arrays layouts: one array per field instead of one array of structs.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Why tracing circuits needs a replacement model
question: Why can't you assign one fixed weight to the edge from an SAE feature before an MLP to an SAE feature after it?
options: SAE features are always dense, so the weight would be huge
The two SAEs use different dictionary sizes
The effect passes through many MLP neurons with nonlinearities, so its size depends on everything else active
Attention moves the feature to a different token position
explain: The MLP mixes the source direction into many neurons, each with a nonlinearity, so the downstream effect changes with the input, as the toy showed (2.846 instead of 1.085 at scale 3). Transcoders sidestep this by replacing the MLP itself with sparse features.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Validating a graph with interventions
question: Why does constrained patching over layers [i, j] avoid double counting a cross-layer feature's effect?
options: It edits the feature's decoding at each layer in the range and does not recompute MLP outputs inside the range, so the only change there is the intervention
It recomputes every MLP inside the range so the feature's effect is applied once
It removes attention for the duration of the range
It only patches the final layer, where all decoders meet
explain: A CLT feature writes to many layers. Editing its decoder outputs across the range while not recomputing MLPs inside that range means the only change to those MLP outputs is your edit. Knock-on effects appear only after the range ends.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Inverse propensity scoring turns clicks into unbiased labels
question: Which statement about the IPS estimator is correct?
options: It needs propensities for unclicked documents too
It is unbiased only if the same query repeats many times
It needs the logged ranking to be random
It is unbiased per query instance, so sparse queries are fine
explain: The proof works per query instance: the expectation over examination of c/theta is gamma for each instance. That is why IPS suits sparse logs like personal search (people searching their own email or files), where classic per-pair click models fail. Unclicked documents contribute zero, so their propensities are not needed.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Reflected XSS: the server echoes the attack back
question: Which log is most likely to contain evidence of a reflected XSS attempt?
options: The database's slow query log
The web server's access log, since the payload is part of the requested URL
The browser's localStorage
No log: reflected payloads never reach the server
explain: Reflected XSS needs the server to echo the payload, so the payload must be in the request, usually the query string. Access logs and WAF logs record it. That is not true of DOM XSS through the URL fragment, which never leaves the browser (lesson 4).

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Framework auto-escaping and its escape hatches
question: An Angular developer calls `bypassSecurityTrustHtml(comment)` because the sanitiser was removing a `style` attribute users wanted. What changed?
options: Nothing, because Angular still sanitises behind the scenes
Angular now inserts the comment without sanitising it, so any markup in it, including event handlers, reaches the DOM
Only styles are now allowed through
The comment is now encoded twice
explain: The bypass functions tell Angular a value is already safe, and Angular's docs say it then does not sanitise it. The fix for a missing feature is to configure a sanitiser to allow exactly what is needed, not to turn sanitisation off.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Stopping CSRF: SameSite, tokens, Origin and Fetch Metadata
question: A server puts its CSRF token only in a cookie and checks that the cookie is present on each POST. Why does this not help?
options: Cookies are encrypted, so the server cannot read the token
The browser attaches the cookie to the forged request automatically, so its presence proves nothing about where the request came from
Tokens must be at least 512 bits long
The attacker can read the cookie through the same-origin policy
explain: A token only works when the request must carry it in a place the attacker cannot fill: a form field or header. OWASP says cookie-only validation is insecure for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to client-side attacks
question: Which sensor can detect a DOM XSS that reads `location.hash`?
options: The WAF in front of the site
CSP or Trusted Types violation reports sent by the victim's browser
The web server's access log
The database audit log
explain: The fragment never reaches the server, so server-side sensors are blind. The browser enforces CSP and Trusted Types where the code runs and reports violations, which makes those reports the only reliable signal for this class.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Zero-shot classification with prompts, probes and robustness
question: You build a zero-shot classifier for 3 product categories and it often confuses two of them. Which change follows CLIP's recipe and costs nothing per prediction?
options: Average the normalized embeddings of several prompt templates per class, renormalize, and cache them
Run the image encoder once per prompt and average the image embeddings
Lower the logit scale from 100 to 1 so the softmax is less confident
Replace the softmax with an argmax over raw cosines
explain: Ensembling in embedding space gives one cached vector per class, so inference cost equals a single prompt, and the paper reports it reliably helps. The image is encoded once regardless of prompts. Changing the scale or using argmax leaves the ranking, and so the confusions, unchanged.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: The shared responsibility model, and when the provider gets it wrong
question: After ChaosDB, what did Microsoft ask potentially affected Cosmos DB customers to do?
options: Nothing, the provider fixed it entirely
Delete their databases
Regenerate their primary read-write keys
Disable Azure Active Directory
explain: Microsoft disabled the notebook feature and asked customers whose keys might have been exposed to regenerate the primary read-write key. A provider bug still left a credential that only the customer could rotate.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Long-lived keys vs temporary credentials: STS and Uber 2016
question: A role's trust policy allows the `ci-deployer` role to assume it, and its permissions policy allows `s3:*`. Which statement is true?
options: The trust policy limits which S3 buckets the session can use
The trust policy lets ci-deployer use S3 directly without assuming the role
ci-deployer can call AssumeRole on it and the resulting session can use S3
Anyone in the account can assume it, because trust policies only apply across accounts
explain: The trust policy decides who may become the role; the permissions policy decides what the role session may do. Together: ci-deployer may assume it, and the session may use S3.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Storage exposure: public buckets, Block Public Access and SAS tokens
question: Why was the 2023 Microsoft SAS token so dangerous compared with a typical shared link?
options: It was signed with a weak hash
It used HTTP instead of HTTPS
It covered the whole storage account with full control and expired in 2051, and SAS creation is not logged, so nobody could see it existed
It required MFA that attackers could bypass
explain: Scope (whole account), permissions (full control) and lifetime (decades) made it equivalent to the account key, and because SAS generation cannot be audited, the owners had no inventory of it.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Catching misconfigurations early: infrastructure as code and CSPM
question: Checkov reports CKV_AWS_79 for an instance resource. What is the fix?
options: Attach a larger instance type
Encrypt the root volume
Add metadata_options with http_tokens = "required" so the instance only accepts IMDSv2
Remove the instance's IAM role
explain: CKV_AWS_79 checks that IMDSv1 is not enabled. Requiring session tokens on the instance resource satisfies it and closes the plain-GET path to role credentials.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
question: A colleague plots inertia for k = 2 to 10, sees the steepest bend at k = 4, and says the data has four clusters. What is the strongest objection?
options: Inertia should go up with k, so their plot must be wrong
The elbow depends on the axis scaling and on the range of k plotted, and the same shape appears even for uniform data with no clusters
They should have used inertia divided by n, which would move the elbow to the right
Four clusters cannot be checked without ground truth labels
explain: Schubert's point: the curve looks the same on well separated blobs, on 25 blobs and on uniform noise, so a bend is not evidence of structure. Rescaling the data multiplies SSE by a squared and moves the apparent elbow, and starting the plot at k = 2 instead of k = 1 changes it again. Inertia does decrease with k, and dividing by n changes nothing about the shape.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Why analytic scans want columns, not rows
question: A dashboard query computes AVG(amount) and COUNT(*) grouped by region over 500 million rows of a 40-column table. What is the main reason a columnar layout helps?
options: It reads only the 2 needed columns instead of all 40, cutting bytes scanned roughly 20x
Column stores keep an index on every column, so the scan becomes index lookups
Each row is stored contiguously, so the CPU prefetcher works better
Columnar files are always smaller because they skip null values
explain: The query touches region and amount only. A column layout lets the scan skip the other 38 columns entirely, so it moves about 2/40 of the bytes (less after compression). No per-column index is needed; the win is the layout itself.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors
question: After Select, a vector of 1024 rows has a selection vector of length 900. The next primitive computes price x quantity. Which is the usual behavior?
options: It loops over the 900 positions in the selection vector and writes results at those same positions
It first copies the 900 rows into new contiguous vectors, then computes
It computes all 1024 rows and Select is re-applied afterwards
It switches to tuple-at-a-time for the selected rows
explain: X100 primitives accept an optional selection vector and compute only for those positions, writing at the same positions, because leaving the child's vectors intact is usually cheaper than copying the selected data.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Vectorization and why -O2 and -O3 differ on loops
question: A loop over `float *out, const float *in` with a runtime length n is not vectorized at `gcc -O2` but is at -O3. What is the most likely reason?
options: -O2 does not support SIMD instructions
-O2's very-cheap cost model rejects loops that need a runtime alias check
Floats can never be vectorized at -O2
The loop needs -march=native first
explain: With runtime n and two pointers that may overlap, vectorizing needs a runtime overlap check. The very-cheap model used at -O2 refuses any runtime alias check (and, before GCC 15, any loop needing a scalar epilogue); -O3's dynamic model accepts them. restrict (plus a known trip count on GCC 14 and older) can make -O2 vectorize it.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
question: A model returns a response with three tool_use blocks: left_click, type, screenshot. What should the harness send back?
options: Only the screenshot image, since that is the observation the model needs
One tool_result per tool_use block, in one user message, matched by tool_use_id
Nothing yet: wait for the model to send each action in a separate turn
A text summary of the three actions written by the harness
explain: The docs require one tool_result for every tool_use block, all in the next user message and matched by tool_use_id. A request that leaves any block unanswered is rejected. The click and type results can be a short OK; the screenshot result is the image.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Why long tasks fail: compounding errors and verification
question: Which verification step best catches a failed "save the report as PDF" task?
options: Checking that the file exists at the expected path with a PDF header and non-zero size
Asking the model whether it thinks it saved the file
Checking that the last action was a click on the Save button
Taking a screenshot and confirming the Save dialog is no longer open
explain: A closed dialog or a Save click does not prove a file was written (the dialog may have been cancelled, or the path may be wrong). Checking the resulting state is what OSWorld's evaluators do and what the vendor docs recommend before reporting success.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Preemption bounds, weak memory and what loom cannot see
question: A loom test of a seqlock (a lock where readers retry if a writer bumped a sequence counter) that uses `store(.., SeqCst)` panics, but you are confident the algorithm is correct under C11. What is the most likely explanation?
options: loom found a real bug that hardware hides
The preemption bound was set too high
loom does not support SeqCst at all and always panics
loom treats SeqCst loads and stores as AcqRel, so it may explore executions that SeqCst forbids, producing a false alarm
explain: The README lists this exact limitation. Check whether the failing execution relies on a reordering SeqCst would forbid; fence(SeqCst) is modeled correctly, plain SeqCst accesses are weakened.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: The boundary condition and the c_skip, c_out parameterization
question: A teammate drops c_skip and c_out and uses f(x, t) = F(x, t) directly, trained with the consistency loss only. What is the main risk?
options: Training becomes slower but converges to the same solution
Nothing ties the outputs to data, so a constant output such as f = 0 minimizes the loss
The model can no longer be sampled in one step
The ODE solver in the teacher becomes unstable
explain: Self-consistency only says outputs agree along a trajectory; a constant function agrees everywhere. The boundary condition f(x, eps) = x anchors the chain to real data, and the paper states it precludes the trivial solution. (Song et al. also allow a piecewise version that returns x at t = eps, but some anchor is required.)

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Linearizability: one copy, respecting real time
question: Your service keeps each key linearizable on its own, using a separate replica group per key. A teammate worries that a history mixing single-key operations on many keys is therefore not linearizable as a whole. What does locality say?
options: Per-key linearizability implies the whole history of single-key operations is linearizable
The teammate is right; you need a global lock across groups
Locality only holds for sequential consistency
It depends on clock synchronization between groups
explain: Herlihy and Wing's Theorem 1: a history is linearizable if and only if each object's sub-history is. This covers single-key operations. An atomic operation that touches two keys at once is a different object (or a transaction), which locality does not cover.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key
question: A cache tier uses hash mod N with 10 servers. One server crashes and clients switch to mod 9. Roughly what fraction of cache lookups now go to a server that does not hold the key?
options: About 10%, only the dead server's keys
About 50%
About 90%
None, because the hash function did not change
explain: Going from 10 to 9 has the same structure as 9 to 10: only 1 in 10 hash values gives the same remainder mod 9 and mod 10, so about 90% of keys move. Losing one server makes nearly the whole cache miss at once, which is exactly the kind of stampede that knocks over the database behind it.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Must-haves and nice-to-haves need different machinery
question: Which requirement is the best candidate for a soft constraint rather than a hard filter?
options: Candidate has the security clearance the contract legally requires
Candidate has not opted out of being contacted by recruiters
Candidate profile is in the recruiter's licensed country
Candidate lives within commuting distance of the office
explain: Distance is a matter of degree: 12 km is a bit worse than 3 km, not a disqualification. Legal, contractual and consent rules are binary and must never be traded for other strengths, so they belong in hard filters.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Why scheduling explodes, and what a constraint model is
question: You add a fifth job E with the same three slots. How many complete assignments must generate and test consider now?
options: 84, since one variable adds three new values
243, since the count multiplies by the domain size
324, since it multiplies by the number of variables
125, which is five jobs raised to three slots
explain: The count is $d^n$. Going from $n=4$ to $n=5$ with $d=3$ multiplies it by 3: $81 \times 3 = 243$. Each new variable multiplies the space, which is why enumeration collapses so quickly.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
question: A constraint says 0.3 x + 0.5 y <= 4 with x, y integers. How should it go into CP-SAT?
options: Pass it as written; CP-SAT converts floats internally to exact rationals
Round each coefficient to the nearest integer: 0 x + 1 y <= 4
Multiply through by 10: 3 x + 5 y <= 40
Replace it with x + y <= 4, which is equivalent
explain: The docs state CP-SAT works over the integers, so non-integer coefficients must be scaled by a large enough integer. Multiplying both sides by 10 keeps exactly the same feasible set. Rounding changes the constraint, and option D drops the weights entirely.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pinning by digest, signing images and verifying at admission
question: A pod spec uses `image: shop/web:1.4`. The image was signed and scanned when 1.4 was first pushed. What risk remains?
options: The tag can later be pointed at different bytes, which were never scanned, and no signature check runs unless admission enforces it
The kubelet re-verifies signatures on every pull by default
Tags expire after 30 days
None, because it was signed
explain: Signing at push time does nothing unless something verifies at deploy time, and a tag can be moved. Pin the digest and enforce signature verification in admission.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: RBAC: roles, bindings and the permissions that escalate
question: A RoleBinding in namespace dev references the ClusterRole secret-reader. Where can the subject read Secrets?
options: Nowhere; RoleBindings cannot reference ClusterRoles
In every namespace, because it is a ClusterRole
Only in kube-system
Only in dev, because a RoleBinding grants within its own namespace
explain: The RBAC docs give this exact example: a RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole, and the binding's namespace decides where the rights apply. Only a ClusterRoleBinding grants cluster-wide.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Network policies: from default allow to default deny
question: After applying default-deny-all, every app fails with name resolution errors, but the allow rules between apps look right. What is missing?
options: Nothing; restart the pods
An ingress rule on the DNS pods
An egress rule allowing UDP and TCP port 53 to the cluster DNS pods
A ClusterRoleBinding for DNS
explain: Default deny for egress also blocks DNS queries, as the docs warn. Add an egress allow to the cluster DNS service on port 53.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime detection with Falco and the Kubernetes audit log
question: Which event would appear in the Kubernetes audit log but not necessarily in Falco?
options: A write to /etc/ld.so.preload
A shell spawned in a container through an anonymous kubelet
A service account listing all Secrets through the API server
A miner connecting to a pool
explain: Listing Secrets is an API request, recorded by the audit log, and produces no unusual process activity on a node for a syscall sensor to see. The others happen on nodes, outside the API server.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: cgroup v2: cpu.max throttling and memory.max kills
question: Which pairing correctly matches a cgroup v2 limit to what happens when a workload pushes past it?
options: cpu.max kills the process; memory.max throttles it
cpu.max stalls the threads until the next period; memory.max reclaims first, then OOM kills inside the cgroup
Both throttle: allocations are slowed to the configured rate
Both kill: the OOM killer handles CPU overuse as well
explain: CPU is compressible, so the kernel can withhold it and let the workload continue more slowly. Memory is not: once reclaim fails there is nothing left to withhold, so the cgroup's OOM killer runs and memory.events records the oom_kill. memory.high is the one memory knob that throttles rather than killing.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Why a multi-turn search needs explicit state
question: Which product is the best fit for explicit slot-based state tracking rather than pure query rewriting?
options: A job search with filters for role, level, location, remote and salary
An open-domain assistant answering follow-up questions about history
A chatbot that summarizes a single uploaded PDF
A spell checker
explain: Slot-based tracking needs a schema of constraints. The job search has one, which puts it on the task-oriented side of the line the CIS survey draws. Open-domain QA has no fixed schema and usually relies on rewriting.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Storing state server-side and measuring it
question: Your app stores only the chat transcript and re-derives state each turn. A user removes the remote filter by clicking its chip, then types *show staff roles too*. What is the likely bug?
options: The click is lost: the re-derived state brings remote back because the transcript still says only remote ones
The query builder crashes on a missing slot
Joint goal accuracy cannot be computed
There is no bug; re-derivation handles UI edits automatically
explain: UI edits are not in the transcript unless you write them there. Re-deriving from text alone resurrects the removed filter. Either log UI events into the history or keep server-side state that the click updates directly.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
question: A lab wants CoTs shown to users to be free of offensive content. Which approach best preserves monitorability?
options: Add a reward penalty whenever the raw CoT contains offensive content
Fine-tune the CoT on curated, polite reasoning traces
Leave the raw CoT unpressured and show users a summary written by a separate model
Shorten the CoT with a length penalty so there is less to filter
explain: Penalizing or curating the raw CoT puts direct pressure on it, which Baker et al. show can teach the model to hide content rather than not have it. A length penalty pushes reasoning into activations. A separate summarizer meets the presentation need while the raw CoT stays free for monitoring.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Streams, the default stream trap, and events
question: A GPU reports asyncEngineCount = 1. You run two streams, each doing an H2D copy and a kernel. What overlap can you expect?
options: The two H2D copies run concurrently with each other and with the kernels
No overlap at all; one copy engine means strictly serial execution
Copies overlap only if both source buffers are in the same pinned allocation
One H2D copy at a time, but a copy can overlap with a kernel
explain: The best practices guide ties this to asyncEngineCount: a GPU with one copy engine can perform one transfer and execute kernels concurrently, while two copy engines additionally allow a host to device and a device to host transfer at the same time. Streams give permission to overlap; the engine count caps how much overlap the hardware can deliver.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
question: A team wants to replace their bi-encoder with a cross-encoder for first-stage retrieval over 20 million passages. What is the core problem?
options: Cross-encoders cannot handle passages longer than a sentence
Every query would need 20 million transformer forward passes, because no document computation can be done ahead of time
Cross-encoders need the documents to be pre-embedded with the same model first
Cross-encoders only work with BM25 candidates
explain: The cross-encoder's document token states depend on the query, so nothing can be precomputed. Scoring a full corpus means one forward pass per document per query, which is why it is used only on a shortlist from a first stage.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Training a reranker: pointwise, pairwise, listwise and hard negatives
question: In the listwise softmax view, which candidate in our group receives the largest gradient pushing its score down?
options: The easy negative at -4.0
The positive at 2.0
The hard negative at 1.5
All negatives receive equal gradient
explain: For softmax cross-entropy the gradient on each negative's logit is its probability: 0.331 for z = 1.5, 0.122 for 0.5 and 0.001 for the easy one. The loss focuses on whichever negatives currently compete with the positive.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Encoding, hashing and encryption are three different things
question: A colleague stores API tokens Base64-encoded in the database "so they are not in plain text". What does an attacker who dumps the table need to use the tokens?
options: The encryption key from the application server
A large brute-force search of the token space
Nothing beyond a Base64 decoder, which every language ships
The hash salt
explain: Base64 is an encoding with no key. Decoding is instant and public. The tokens are effectively stored in plain text.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Authenticated encryption: AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and nonce reuse
question: A service encrypts with AES-GCM but uses a fixed nonce of 12 zero bytes for every message. What is lost?
options: Nothing, because GCM authenticates every message
Only the secrecy of the first message
Confidentiality of messages that share the nonce, and the ability to trust any tag under that key
Only performance
explain: Repeated nonce means repeated keystream (plaintext XORs leak) and, per SP 800-38D Appendix A, likely recovery of the hash subkey, which lets an attacker forge tags. Both secrecy and integrity fail.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Password hashing and key derivation: slow on purpose
question: Why is a per-user random salt essential even with a slow hash?
options: It makes each hash faster to verify
It replaces the need for a slow hash
Without it, users with the same password share a hash, so one guess tests all of them and precomputed tables work
It encrypts the password
explain: Salts make every user's hash unique, forcing the attacker to attack each account separately and defeating precomputation. Slowness then multiplies the cost of each separate attack.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Elliptic curves and digital signatures: the PS3 and CurveBall
question: Two ECDSA signatures from the same key have the same r value. What does that tell you?
options: Nothing; r often repeats
The messages were identical
The same per-message secret k was used, and the private key can be computed from the two signatures
The curve is broken
explain: r is the x-coordinate of kG, so equal r means equal k (for practical purposes). Then the two s equations solve for k and the private key, as with the PS3.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Layout algebra: composition, tiling and partitioning
question: In the CuTe GEMM tutorial, a CTA calls local_tile(mA, tiler, coord) and each thread then calls local_partition(gA, tA, threadIdx.x). What does each call keep?
options: local_tile keeps the tile mode and slices the rest; local_partition slices the tile mode and keeps the rest
Both keep the tile mode
local_tile keeps the rest mode; local_partition keeps the tile mode
Both keep the rest mode
explain: local_tile (inner partition) indexes the rest mode with the CTA coordinate and keeps one whole tile. local_partition (outer partition) indexes inside the tile with the thread index and keeps the repeats, so a thread gets one element per repeat of the thread tile.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
question: A host has all 64 cores rented to VMs and 100 GB of DRAM still free. Which statement is correct?
options: The 100 GB is stranded: no core is left to pair with it, so it cannot be rented until a VM leaves
The 100 GB is fine: the next VM to arrive can use it
The 100 GB will be swapped out to free space for other hosts
The 100 GB is lost only if the host is a NUMA machine
explain: VMs need cores and memory together. With zero free cores, no new VM fits on this host, so the free DRAM is paid for but unsellable. That is the definition of stranded memory that motivates pooling.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
question: With demotion enabled, a server's local DRAM node hits its low watermark. What happens to a cold anonymous page that would previously have gone to swap?
options: It is migrated to the CXL node and stays mapped, so a later access is a slower load rather than a page-in from disk
It is compressed into zswap on the local node
It is dropped and re-read from the executable file
It is moved to the CXL node but unmapped until a page fault brings it back to DRAM
explain: Demotion uses page migration in the reclaim path: the page moves to the next slower tier and the page tables are updated. The program can still load it directly, just with CXL latency.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The 3-step pipeline and what it did to The Pile
question: Which step of DoReMi needs the Group DRO optimizer?
options: Only step 3, the large main model
Steps 1 and 3
All three steps
Only step 2, the small proxy model
explain: Step 1 is ordinary training of the reference model, and step 3 is ordinary training of the main model on resampled data. Only the small proxy in step 2 uses the min-max objective, which is why the expensive run needs no special code.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Counting cache lines: the traffic model and the padding bonus
question: Which workload is the best fit for keeping AoS?
options: Summing one numeric field over every row
Finding all records whose flag byte is set
Fetching a random record by id and returning all of its fields
Running the same arithmetic on x, y and z of every point with SIMD
explain: Random access to whole records uses every byte of the one line AoS brings in, while SoA would touch one line per field. The other three stream a few fields over many records, which is exactly where SoA (or blocked SoA for SIMD) wins.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Two orderings, two answers: float addition is not associative
question: A kernel sums 4096 float32 products. You pin the reduction so that every run uses the same tree in the same order. What have you guaranteed?
options: The result now equals the exact mathematical sum.
The same inputs give the same bits on every run of the same build and hardware, although the result is still not the exact sum.
The result is now within one ulp of the exact sum.
Any other implementation of the same sum will now agree with you bitwise.
explain: Fixing the order buys reproducibility, not accuracy. The rounding errors are still there; they are simply the same errors every time. A different kernel with a different tree is equally valid IEEE 754 and will generally give different bits.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
question: A cached and an uncached run emit different token ids but detokenize to the same text. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The cache is broken and the test should fail.
The test should only ever compare at the text level, since text is what users receive.
Users are unaffected, but the numerics genuinely differ, so a logit-level or bitwise test is the one that will localize the cause.
The tokenizer is nondeterministic and should be reseeded.
explain: Identical text with different ids is possible, so text equality is the weakest of the three levels. It is the right contract to promise a user and the wrong instrument for finding the cause, which lives in the logits. Compare at the logit level to localize, then state the guarantee at the level you actually promise.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Knowing a run went wrong: invariants, oracles and liveness
question: Your DST suite injects only crashes that always restart within 2 simulated seconds and partitions that always heal within 5. Which bug is it most likely to miss?
options: Two leaders committing different values in the same term
A follower that never catches up while one peer stays permanently down
A torn write corrupting the log
An off-by-one in log index comparison
explain: That is a liveness bug, and it hides whenever faults heal on their own, exactly as in TigerBeetle's resonance bug. The other options are safety violations that can show up under transient faults. To catch liveness bugs, make some faults permanent and require a healthy quorum to keep making progress.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Runners: where pipeline code runs, and how to isolate it
question: A team runs self-hosted runners and adds a script that wipes and re-images each VM after a job finishes. GitHub's guidance says this is weaker than it looks. Why?
options: Re-imaging is too slow to matter
GitHub-hosted runners are never wiped either
Wiping removes the runner's registration token, which breaks the next job
Nothing guarantees the runner took only one job before the wipe, so a second job (possibly privileged) can still land on a dirty machine; JIT runners are registered for exactly one job
explain: The secure use reference says automatic destruction might not be as effective as intended because there is no way to guarantee a self-hosted runner only runs one job. A just-in-time runner is removed by GitHub after at most one job.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Caches and artifacts: how Ultralytics was poisoned
question: A pull_request_target workflow checks out PR code but has a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN and no secrets. Before GitHub's cache restrictions, what could still go wrong?
options: The PR code could use the job's cache token to write cache entries under main's scope, which a later release workflow would restore
Nothing: a read-only token cannot change anything
The PR could merge itself
The runner would crash
explain: This is exactly Adnan Khan's finding: the runtime cache token is separate from GITHUB_TOKEN. Writing into main's cache scope turned a low-privilege job into code inside the release.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Policy as code with OPA and Rego
question: In Rego, a rule body has five lines. Four are true for a resource and one is false. What happens?
options: The rule does not fire for that resource, because lines in a body are joined by AND
The rule fires, since most lines are true
Rego raises an error
The rule fires once for each true line
explain: All lines in a body must hold for the same choice of variables. To express OR, write a second rule with the same name.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a secure pipeline, a response plan, practice
